questions.stem: During labour, the hormone oxytocin stimulates uterine contractions, which in turn cause more oxytocin to be released. This is an example of:

options.text: Negative feedback, because the contractions eventually stop after birth
Homeostasis, because the body is maintaining a constant internal state
Positive feedback, because the response amplifies the original stimulus
A reflex arc, because it is an automatic involuntary response

questions.explanation: This is positive feedback: oxytocin causes contractions, which push the baby against the cervix, stimulating more oxytocin release, causing stronger contractions. The response amplifies itself until birth occurs. This is different from negative feedback, which works to restore a system to its original state.

questions.stem: A doctor notices that a woman in labour has stopped dilating at 6 cm and contractions have slowed. They administer synthetic oxytocin via a drip. What is the intended effect?

options.text: To reduce pain so the mother can rest
To strengthen and increase the frequency of uterine contractions, helping the cervix to dilate fully
To cause the placenta to detach from the uterus wall
To relax the cervix so the baby can pass through more easily

questions.explanation: Synthetic oxytocin (Syntocinon/Pitocin) mimics the natural hormone that stimulates uterine contractions. Administering it strengthens and increases the frequency of contractions, helping the cervix to continue dilating to the full 10 cm needed for the baby to pass through the birth canal.

questions.stem: During a normal birth, the baby is typically delivered head-first. A breech presentation, where the baby's feet or bottom come first, may require a caesarean section. Why is a head-first delivery safer?

options.text: The head is the smallest part of the baby and passes through the cervix most easily
The head is the largest part and dilates the birth canal for the rest of the body to follow; in breech position the head may become trapped
Head-first delivery ensures the baby breathes immediately
The umbilical cord is less likely to be cut in a head-first delivery

questions.explanation: The baby's head is the largest part. When delivered head-first, it stretches the birth canal wide enough for the shoulders and body to follow. In a breech presentation, the body delivers first but the larger head may become trapped in the birth canal, which can compress the umbilical cord and cut off the baby's blood and oxygen supply.

questions.stem: After the baby is born, the placenta is delivered as the afterbirth. Why is it medically important to check that the entire placenta has been expelled?

options.text: Retained placental tissue can cause continued bleeding and serious infection in the mother
The placenta needs to be tested to determine the baby's blood group
Any remaining placenta will begin producing hormones that harm the baby
The placenta must be removed so the mother can begin breastfeeding

questions.explanation: If fragments of the placenta remain attached to the uterus wall, the uterus cannot contract fully, leading to postpartum haemorrhage (heavy bleeding). Retained tissue can also become infected, causing a serious condition. Medical staff carefully examine the placenta after delivery to confirm it is complete.

questions.stem: Immediately after birth, the umbilical cord is clamped and cut. Why does the baby not feel pain when the cord is cut?

options.text: The baby is given pain relief before the cord is cut
The umbilical cord contains no nerve fibres, so there are no pain receptors
The baby's nervous system is not developed enough to feel pain
The cord is cut so quickly that the pain signals cannot travel to the brain

questions.explanation: The umbilical cord does not contain nerve fibres, so neither the mother nor the baby feels pain when it is cut. The cord contains the umbilical vein and arteries surrounded by a jelly-like substance (Wharton's jelly), but no sensory nerves.
